section_summary: This section assembles editorials, religious statements, private correspondence, company replies, diplomatic reports, and cross-reference sheets concerning American exports of petroleum, scrap metal, aircraft, and other strategic materials to Japan. Much of the material urges an embargo or other economic sanctions in response to Japan’s war in China, while State Department replies explain existing neutrality policy and the limits of executive authority. The section concludes with a lengthy Legal Adviser’s memorandum examining whether the Nine-Power Treaty or international law empowered the President to prohibit shipments to Japan without additional legislation.

subfiles.title: [Article arguing against isolationism and moral neutrality]
subfiles.about: The article argues that the United States should oppose aggressor states economically and support peace-loving nations.
subfiles.summary: The writer rejects isolationism and contends that neutrality between aggression and its victims is immoral. Citing Ethiopia, China, Bohemia, Moravia, and Albania, the article urges the United States to stop trading with aggressors and to sell munitions only to states defending peace.

subfiles.title: Does Japan Understand Now?
subfiles.about: The editorial welcomes denunciation of the 1911 U.S.-Japan treaty and calls for an embargo on war-making materials.
subfiles.summary: Editorial: Japan may now grasp American displeasure after the treaty notice; it condemns scrap iron and machinery sales to Japan, especially from Boston, and calls for naming the firms.

subfiles.title: Participation in Aggression
subfiles.from: G. Ashton Oldham and other religious leaders
subfiles.about: Religious leaders declare that supplying aggressor nations constitutes participation in aggression.
subfiles.summary: Two hundred Protestant, Catholic and Jewish leaders urge ending American economic support for aggressor states in six principles opposing war and discrimination and backing relief and concerted opposition to aggression.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to Bethlehem Steel concerning shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: A shareholder asks whether Bethlehem Steel products are being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: McKee asks Bethlehem Steel not to be indifferent to strengthening an aggressor that raised U.S. defense costs, suggesting shareholders would sacrifice profits from Japanese business.

subfiles.title: Bethlehem Steel reply concerning Japanese sales
subfiles.about: Bethlehem Steel acknowledges substantial exports to Japan but opposes unilateral corporate restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Bethlehem Steel says it shipped substantial ordinary commercial steel to Japan in 1937-1938, competitors would replace withheld sales, and restrictions belong to the national government.

subfiles.title: Atlantic Refining reply concerning shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Atlantic Refining states that none of its products are being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The company acknowledges McKee’s inquiry about exports to Japan. Its answer is an unequivocal negative.

subfiles.title: Gulf Oil reply concerning Japanese business
subfiles.about: Gulf Oil defends its small, longstanding trade with Japanese customers.
subfiles.summary: Gulf Oil says Japan is a satisfactory market with excellent credit, its sales are small, negligible to the hostilities, and will continue under company policy.

subfiles.title: Texas Gulf Sulphur reply concerning shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Texas Gulf Sulphur denies that it has ever shipped its products to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Texas Gulf Sulphur replies that it is not shipping products to Japan and never has.

subfiles.title: Union Carbide reply concerning Japanese sales
subfiles.about: Union Carbide describes its sales to Japan as limited quantities of industrial carbon products and organic chemicals.
subfiles.summary: Union Carbide says its Japanese trade is carbon products and organic chemicals for general industry in small quantities.

subfiles.title: United Aircraft reply concerning sales to Japan
subfiles.about: United Aircraft acknowledges occasional Japanese purchases, including one airplane.
subfiles.summary: United Aircraft says it sold certain products to Japan over twelve years, including one airplane years earlier.

subfiles.title: International Nickel reply concerning sales in Japan
subfiles.about: International Nickel explains that it sells globally, including in Japan, and cannot readily control the ultimate use of nickel.
subfiles.summary: International Nickel says its products are used worldwide, including Japan, mostly by peacetime industry, and refers McKee to Stanley's shareholder address.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on extending the moral embargo
subfiles.about: The State Department declines to extend its aircraft moral-embargo policy to all manufacturers and exporters of war materials.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges McKee’s suggestion that the Department ask exporters of war materials to refrain from selling to Japan. He explains that the aircraft policy rested on the exceptional circumstance of aerial bombing of civilians and that the Department takes advisory action of this kind only in such exceptional cases.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on C. T. Takahashi and Company
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a postal inspection report on a Seattle Japanese import-export firm’s dealings in scrap iron and rubber.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a postal report on C. T. Takahashi and Company of Seattle and its scrap iron and rubber transactions.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to protest over the Chengdu bombing
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram protesting Japanese bombing and American material assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a protest over indiscriminate Japanese bombing, especially Chengdu, asking immediate prohibition of indirect American assistance to Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting the bombing of Chengdu
subfiles.about: Missionaries report a devastating Japanese air raid on Chengdu and demand an end to American supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports that twenty-six bombers struck densely populated Chengdu and dropped bombs on the American- and British-owned West China Union University campus. It lists casualties, including an American woman, denies that military objectives were present, and says continued American sales of gasoline and iron make such attacks possible.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Joseph A. Shirley letter on destruction in China
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a letter condemning Japan’s destruction of China with the aid of American materials.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Joseph Shirley's letter asking what steps the U.S. will take as American materials assist Japan's destruction of China.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to reply on shipments of war materials to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a letter explaining the Department’s attitude toward shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a reply stating the State Department's position on exports to Japan, with supporting documents.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on the Japanese vessel Erimo
subfiles.about: The sheet reports that the Japanese vessel Erimo loaded scrap iron and other cargo at Honolulu without proper manifest or clearance.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Commerce asked State to act after the Japanese vessel Erimo took cargo without filing a manifest or obtaining clearance.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Adeline W. Owen protest
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a letter condemning American sales and shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Adeline Owen's protest against trade in materials useful to Japan's war.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Senator Schwellenbach’s brief
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a senatorial letter and brief on materials used by Japan in its war against China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Senator Schwellenbach's brief on American shipments to Japan, for consideration of restricting goods used in China.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for enclosure 708
subfiles.about: An administrative slip records the removal or charging of an enclosure from file 894.24.
subfiles.summary: Charge slip for enclosure 708 with a 1947 notation; no substantive content.

subfiles.title: Our Oil in Japan’s War Motors
subfiles.about: The editorial argues that American oil and scrap steel sustain Japan’s military power and anti-American posture.
subfiles.summary: Editorial calls it absurd for Japan to buy the materials with which it excludes American business from China, advocating ending oil shipments as national defense.

subfiles.title: Slush Fund and Third-Term Song
subfiles.from: Drew Pearson and Robert A. Allen
subfiles.about: The column alleges that a Spanish cotton loan served corporate interests and also notes a Roosevelt third-term campaign song.
subfiles.summary: Pearson and Allen column: the Export-Import Bank credit to Franco was designed to secure Spanish property interests for ITT and National City Bank; a short item on a third-term campaign song.

subfiles.title: We Can’t Win, but We Might Lose
subfiles.about: The editorial advocates American withdrawal from East Asia to avoid war over limited commercial interests.
subfiles.summary: Editorial: neither a Japanese nor Chinese victory would preserve American commercial privileges; it urges withdrawing gunboats, citizens and businesses and criticizes steel, oil and scrap shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing clippings on China and Spain policy
subfiles.about: Hyslop criticizes the administration’s application of neutrality policy to the wars in China and Spain.
subfiles.summary: Hyslop accuses Roosevelt and Hull of abusing discretion by not recognizing a state of war and embargoing cotton, copper and scrap iron, and attacks the Export-Import Bank credit to Franco.

subfiles.title: Letter protesting aircraft, petroleum, and scrap exports
subfiles.about: Hyslop challenges apparent inconsistencies in U.S. restrictions on exports to Japan and belligerent countries.
subfiles.summary: Hyslop asks why a Douglas DC-4 was being shipped to Japan despite aircraft-license assurances, condemns oil and scrap exports to Japan and Italy, and alleges Spanish cotton would go to Germany.

subfiles.title: Newspaper editorial-page clipping on national defense, Lord Lothian, and militarism
subfiles.about: Three editorial notes criticize exports to potential enemies, examine Lord Lothian’s views, and argue against foreign military adventures.
subfiles.summary: Editorial-page clipping contrasting American rearmament with sales of aircraft, oil, scrap and cotton to Japan, Italy and Spain, plus items on Lord Lothian and militarism.

subfiles.title: [Adjacent memoir excerpt on organized-crime prosecutions]
subfiles.about: An unrelated adjacent column recalls legal discussions and prosecutions involving Lucky Luciano’s associates.
subfiles.summary: Adjacent memoir excerpt on meeting Joe Adonis, Meyer Lansky and Louis Buchalter about the Dewey Law, and racketeering prosecutions.

subfiles.title: Spanish Cotton and War Surprise
subfiles.about: The column alleges that American-financed Spanish cotton was going to Germany and recalls State Department forecasts of the European war.
subfiles.summary: Column: Franco allegedly forwarded Export-Import Bank-financed cotton to Hitler; the State Department anticipated the European war more accurately than newspapers or Congress.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning the Douglas DC-4 and Canada
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the Japanese DC-4 sale did not violate its moral-embargo policy and confirms the Canadian arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: Yost says the Douglas contract predated the June 1938 policy discouraging aircraft sales to countries bombing civilians. He quotes Sumner Welles’s assurance that the policy remained unchanged and notes that the September 10 presidential proclamation prohibited arms exports to Canada.

subfiles.title: Letter requesting data on Japan’s strategic-material imports
subfiles.about: Mrs. Fitch asks for authoritative data on the foreign supplies sustaining Japan’s war machine and advocates the Schwellenbach proposal.
subfiles.summary: Fitch cites estimates that the American share of Japanese war goods rose above fifty-seven percent in 1938, calls the U.S. complicit, and urges restrictions modeled on the Schwellenbach bill.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck reply on Japanese supply statistics
subfiles.about: Hornbeck supplies economic references while cautioning against overstating American responsibility for Japan’s war.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck encloses a Commerce Department report and points to Japanese production statistics, while emphasizing the difficulty of separating military from civilian uses of imported commodities. He objects to calling the United States Japan’s “partner,” arguing that such characterizations are inaccurate and politically counterproductive and that understatement is preferable.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting information on Mexican feldspar and scrap iron
subfiles.about: The American Embassy in Mexico forwards a memorandum on prospective feldspar and scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Daniels transmits Gibson's conversation with shipping executive Burwell on Mexican feldspar and scrap iron shipped from Manzanillo, treated as confidential.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Robert Burwell
subfiles.about: Burwell describes large prospective shipments of Mexican feldspar and railway scrap to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Burwell reports 500 tons of feldspar awaiting shipment, a Japanese option for 2,000 tons monthly, and talks on 80,000-100,000 tons of railway scrap, with Mexico dropping export duties.

subfiles.title: Vice-consular letter transmitting Nagoya Shimbun editorial
subfiles.about: The Nagoya vice consul forwards an editorial advocating immediate shipment of Japan’s gold reserve to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Richardson transmits an August 9 Nagoya Shimbun editorial urging conversion of Japanese gold into materials before a U.S. embargo.

subfiles.title: Send Gold Reserve Immediately
subfiles.about: The editorial urges the Bank of Japan to exchange its gold reserve for productive equipment and strategic resources before American restrictions take effect.
subfiles.summary: Editorial reads Morgenthau's remarks on Japanese bullion as economic pressure after the treaty denunciation and proposes sending the Bank of Japan's entire gold reserve to America to buy resources; breaks off.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to P. D. Boothroyd letter advocating sanctions
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a Pacific Northwest appeal for every possible sanction against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to P. D. Boothroyd's letter condemning munitions sales to a predatory government and noting strong Pacific Northwest support for sanctions.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting Far Eastern policy memorandum
subfiles.about: Price forwards a memorandum reassessing the Far East after the outbreak of war in Europe.
subfiles.summary: Price invites Hamilton's comments on a Far Eastern policy memorandum, adding that the Russo-Japanese truce may let Japan press China, making America Japan's armorer.

subfiles.title: War in Europe—What About Asia?
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and interested policymakers
subfiles.about: The memorandum argues that the European war has increased Japan’s dependence on the United States and strengthened the case for an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Committee memorandum: Japan is isolated and exposed to Soviet power while Britain and France are distracted; the U.S. is Japan's indispensable supplier, so withholding war materials and aiding China could halt Japanese militarism.

subfiles.title: Hamilton acknowledgment to Harry B. Price
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Price’s memorandum and invites further discussion in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton thanks Price for the Far Eastern policy memorandum and welcomes another talk in Washington.

subfiles.title: Congressional inquiry on trade with Japan and cash-and-carry
subfiles.about: Representative Anderson asks how Congress should answer constituents seeking restrictions on trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Representative Anderson asks whether Congress can stop raw-material and scrap-iron shipments to Japan, how cash-and-carry would affect trade, and whether it favors Japan.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Representative Anderson
subfiles.about: Hull offers an oral briefing by Far Eastern specialists instead of written answers to Anderson’s broad policy questions.
subfiles.summary: Hull suggests Anderson discuss his wide-ranging inquiries with Hamilton and other Far Eastern officials.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Mexican scrap and feldspar exports
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to reports of feldspar and scrap iron accumulated at Mazatlán for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Japanese representatives held options on much Mexican scrap iron, feldspar stocks awaited shipment, and Mexico agreed to waive export tax.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Secretary forwarding legal analysis
subfiles.about: Moore forwards a legal memorandum concluding that the Nine-Power Treaty does not itself authorize a presidential embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Moore says the legal analysis answers Senator Schwellenbach's main question in the negative: no treaty-based embargo authority, though the President might use moral influence on exporters, as with bombing aircraft.

subfiles.title: The Fulfillment of Our Treaty Obligations with China
subfiles.about: The memorandum analyzes whether American shipments to Japan violate obligations to China and whether the President may embargo them without Congress.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum traces Article I of the Nine-Power Treaty from the Root Resolution through conference drafting and Senate ratification, emphasizing statements that its obligations were principally moral, passive, and enforceable through consultation or protest rather than automatic force. It concludes that the promise to respect China’s sovereignty and territorial integrity cannot reasonably be read as an executive grant of authority to prohibit every American article that Japan might use against China. Comparing the treaty with general international-law duties of respect, it further concludes that existing international law did not impose a legally enforceable obligation to stop arms or war-material shipments to aggressor states, however morally desirable such a policy might be.
